evals.prompt: I'm 34, been managing a Verazo Home Goods store in Columbus for six years, $58K salary, and I want out. My cousin makes serious money in real estate here and keeps telling me it's uncapped, so I'm ready to go get licensed and hustle. Only problem is my wife's maternity leave ends and our budget stops working unless I'm earning again by December 1st. We have about $7,200 in savings. What's my move?
evals.expected_output: An interview-first response that treats the sub-3-month date and the thin runway as hard constraints, deletes the licensed real-estate route by name rather than ranking it last, presents 2-3 surviving paths with a stated ordering and benchmark-anchored trade-offs, and gates the roadmap on an explicit pick.
expectations: Asks clarifying interview questions before proposing any path, rather than delivering a finished plan in the first reply
Treats December 1 as a hard date under three months and states that this promotes the salaried B2B entry route
Records the licensed real-estate path as deleted and names the constraint that deleted it (the sub-three-month date, the sub-three-month savings runway, or both)
Does not present real estate as an option sitting at the bottom of a ranked menu
Cites the NAR 2026 Member Profile figure that agents with two years or less of experience had a median gross income of about $8,000, naming the publisher
Names the jurisdiction-bound licensing exam, continuing education, and brokerage sponsorship as a compliance cost that the B2B routes do not carry
Presents between two and three surviving paths, never one and never five
States the ordering used for the surviving paths out loud with its axis named, rather than leaving the order implied by list position
Describes each surviving path in a rep's terms: entry difficulty, comp shape, realistic first-two-years income, promotion or book-building timeline, and washout risk
Names the conflict between the user's appetite for an uncapped ceiling and his $7,200 runway, and makes the user resolve it rather than resolving it silently
Closes with exactly one recommendation tied to the user's date, geography, and comp priority
Requires an explicit pick from the user before building any roadmap, and states that passive agreement does not count as a pick

evals.prompt: Quick gut check. I've been an SDR at Palterra (mid-market HR software) for 8 months, hit 112% of my meeting target three quarters running, and my VP just offered me an AE seat starting next month - SMB segment, $85K base, $170K OTE. My roommate says take it before they change their mind. Am I crazy to even hesitate?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against taking the seat at month 8, anchored to the Bridge Group early-promotion failure split and the median time in seat, with a dated decision point and a reframe of the meeting-target number as an input metric.
expectations: Advises against taking the AE seat at month 8 as offered, rather than congratulating the user and confirming the move
Cites the early-promotion failure split: roughly 55% AE failure for SDRs promoted before 11 months against roughly 6% for those with 16+ months in seat
Attributes that split to The Bridge Group as a primary source rather than presenting the figures unattributed or as second-hand
States the study's failure definition (leaving the AE seat within six months) or its sample size (n=205)
Cites the median of about 16 months in an SDR seat before promotion, attributed to Bridge Group
Recommends accumulating roughly 12-16 months of in-seat evidence before taking the AE jump
Mentions the overall SDR-to-AE failure rate of about 26%, the 41% rate for SDRs who changed companies to take the AE role, or both
Notes that this internal promotion avoids the higher failure rate attached to changing companies for an AE seat
Does not claim that three quarters of meeting-target attainment predicts AE success
Treats the 112% meeting-target figure as an activity or input metric and asks for outcome evidence such as pipeline sourced or closed-won influenced
Gives the user a dated decision point for re-opening the AE conversation rather than an open-ended instruction to wait longer
Labels every benchmark used with its publisher and edition rather than stating figures free-floating

evals.prompt: Got an offer from Nuvexa (Series B, revenue intelligence) - mid-market AE, $110K base, $215K OTE, 50/50 split, $900K annual quota, plus 0.08% equity. The recruiter says the team is crushing it right now. My current job pays $150K all-in and is boring. Should I take the $215K?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to value the offer at face OTE, an explicit re-valuation at the team's real attainment, the diligence questions to ask before deciding, and a total-comp comparison against the current $150K.
expectations: Refuses to treat the $215K OTE as $215K and re-values it at the team's real attainment rather than at 100%
Shows the re-valuation arithmetic explicitly: expected variable equals the variable component multiplied by the team attainment rate
Applies the roughly 43% market attainment baseline from the RepVue Cloud Sales Index as the default when the team's own number is unknown
Labels that RepVue baseline as crowdsourced rather than presenting it as a verified published figure
Produces the question asking what percentage of people in this exact role, on this exact team, hit quota last quarter
Produces the quota-capacity question: how many reps carry what quota, against what company goal
States that a refusal to answer the attainment question is itself the answer and should be scored as data
Cites the interpretation band from a VC diligence framework: aggregate attainment of 60-70% is bad numbers, 85-100% is really good
Flags the recruiter's crushing it claim as a headline with no attainment data behind it, matching a documented offer red flag
Instructs the user to build a 25th/50th/75th percentile comp band for the exact role, level, and location, noting each source and its pull date
Compares total compensation (base plus variable at real attainment plus equity plus benefits) against the current $150K rather than comparing base to base
Asks what quota is during ramp and how long ramp lasts before the decision is made
Does not tell the user to accept or decline before the team attainment answer is in hand

evals.prompt: Cleaning up my resume before I apply to AE roles. Tell me if these bullets land: (1) Closed $1.4M in new ARR against a $750K quota, 187% attainment, FY2025. (2) Averaged 22 closed-won deals per year at a $48K average deal size. (3) Exceeded quota every single year since 2022 - 120%, 134%, 151%, 187%. (4) Ran 40+ discovery calls a month. Anything you'd punch up?
evals.expected_output: An arithmetic, provenance, and depth audit of every quantified claim that catches the deal-count mismatch, flags the unbroken 100%+ streak as a red flag, and reframes failing claims instead of polishing or padding them.
expectations: Runs an arithmetic cross-check on the claims rather than only improving their wording
Flags that 22 deals at a $48K average size yields about $1.06M, which does not reconcile with the $1.4M closed figure
Confirms that $1.4M against a $750K quota does compute to roughly 187%, rather than flagging that claim as wrong
Flags four consecutive years of 100%+ attainment as itself a red flag, because fewer than half of reps hit quota in a given year
Refuses to invent, pad, or round any number upward to make a bullet stronger
Applies a provenance check: asks where each number comes from and whether a reference would answer yes to a factual confirmation of it
Applies a depth check: asks whether the user can tell the quarter-level deal story behind the number for about two minutes
Offers the reframing options for a failing claim - a range, a conservative bound, or an input metric - rather than only deleting it
Treats the 40+ discovery calls per month bullet as an input or activity metric and repositions it behind an outcome such as pipeline sourced or meetings converted
States that the evidence audit passes only at 100% of claims and that nothing is deliverable while any claim fails
Names hiring-side verification methods the audit anticipates, such as a math audit, quarterly probes, W-2 cross-checks, or off-list references
States that getting caught padding disqualifies the candidate, rather than treating padding as a stylistic risk
Re-runs the audit after any reframe rather than accepting a rewritten claim as settled

evals.prompt: Helios Ridge Solar in Phoenix offered me a closer role - no base, but a $3,000/month draw and unlimited earning potential, and they say their reps clear $110K. I've got about five weeks of expenses saved and I start Monday if I say yes. Talk me through it.
evals.expected_output: A written draw-terms checklist demanded before acceptance, the runway shortfall named explicitly, the vague comp claim flagged as a red flag, and a warning that the Monday timeline cannot be met responsibly.
expectations: Requires the draw terms in writing before any acceptance, and says so explicitly
Asks whether the $3,000 monthly draw is recoverable or non-recoverable
Requires the recovery schedule in writing: which commissions repay the draw, and at what rate
Requires written treatment of a negative draw balance at separation, naming it as the main source of final-pay disputes
Requires clawback conditions on cancelled or refunded sales, including the clawback window
Requires a lead-flow commitment in measurable terms: who generates the leads and what share of pipeline they are expected to be
States the 3-6 month savings runway requirement before accepting a straight-commission seat and identifies the user's five weeks as falling short of it
Flags unlimited earning potential offered as the only comp statement as a documented B2C offer red flag
Does not accept the reps clear $110K claim at face value as the user's expected income
States that B2C compensation data is thin and directional compared with B2B benchmarks, rather than quoting B2C figures with equal confidence
Advises against saying yes by Monday without the written terms, rather than helping the user decide inside that timeline
Ranks the lead-flow question alongside the team-attainment question for a commission seat, because a commission seat with no lead flow has no attainment worth asking about

evals.prompt: Seven years as a backend engineer working on distributed systems at a payments company, currently $185K. I'm burnt out on writing code and I want the money and the freedom of enterprise sales. My plan is to apply straight to enterprise AE roles at infrastructure vendors since I know the buyer's world cold. How do I position that?
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked entry ordering that routes the technical background through sales engineering or CSM rather than straight to enterprise AE, with the enterprise-AE gate named and the route deleted if it cannot be bridged inside the user's date.
expectations: Recommends routing into sales through sales engineering or a CSM seat rather than applying straight to enterprise AE
Justifies that routing with the fact that sales engineers share accounts with AEs and already know the product, and convert into strong reps
Presents the technical background as a user fact that re-ranks the default entry ordering, not as an exception carved out of it
States the employer gate on enterprise AE seats: prior enterprise selling exposure, which this candidate cannot yet evidence
Deletes the direct enterprise-AE route while naming the constraint that deleted it, if the gate cannot be bridged inside the user's timeframe, rather than ranking it last
Does not claim that domain knowledge of the buyer substitutes for a quota-carrying track record
Presents two to three surviving paths with a stated ordering and its axis named
Gives enterprise AE comp with its benchmark label, roughly $240-320K OTE at a 55:45 to 60:40 split, rather than an unsourced figure
Surfaces the sales-engineer comp anchor (BLS May 2024 mean of about $130,410) against the current $185K so the pay change is visible rather than glossed
Asks for the date by which the move must land, plus the user's effort ceiling and reversibility requirement, before recommending a path

evals.prompt: Final panel at Corvane Analytics next Thursday for an SDR role. It's me, the SDR manager, and a director. I was a barista and shift lead for three years, then did two years of fundraising for a university - I've never carried a sales quota. I asked what to expect and they said a short role-play and some behavioral questions. Help me not blow it.
evals.expected_output: All four candidate artifacts prepared in build order, the role-play identified as the most predictive stage, adjacent quantified proof built from the fundraising and retail numbers, and panel questions drawn from the diligence list.
expectations: Prepares all four candidate artifacts rather than selecting one as most important: a STAR story bank, a mock-call plan, a sell-me-this-pen answer, and a 30-60-90 plan if the employer asks for one
States that the four artifacts are in build order and are not ranked against each other, because each covers a different stage of the loop
Specifies the STAR bank as five competency buckets with each story rehearsed at three lengths: about two minutes, sixty seconds, and fifteen seconds
Includes a miss-and-recovery story in the story bank, not only wins
Requires the sell-me-this-pen answer to qualify with questions before pitching and to end with an explicit ask for the business
Identifies the role-play as the most predictive stage of the loop, citing that it predicts up to about 29% of future job success
Names feature-dumping and passivity as the behaviors interviewers punish
Names discovery questions, listening, adapting to a curveball, and an explicit close as what interviewers reward
Converts the user's fundraising totals and shift-lead retail numbers into quantified adjacent proof, positioned as evidence of persuasion, resilience, and target-hitting
Instructs the user to rehearse the mock call aloud rather than silently
Supplies at least two questions for the user to ask the panel, drawn from the diligence list and starting with the team-level quota attainment question
Warns against questions answerable from the company website, pure comp questions before an offer, and yes/no questions
Warns that having no questions for the panel, or never asking for the close, loses the room

evals.prompt: I'm an SDR at Brightloom and I'm interviewing internally for the AE seat. Two things: first, draft the 30-60-90 I'll present in the panel. Second, since I'll basically be helping them design this role anyway, write the interview scorecard they should grade me on and the ramp plan the company should put new AEs on.
evals.expected_output: The candidate-authored 30-60-90 plan produced and anchored to benchmarks and named accounts, with the employer scorecard and company ramp plan declined as hiring-side work and routed to the sibling hiring skill.
expectations: Produces the candidate-authored 30-60-90 plan as an interview deliverable
Declines to produce the employer's interview scorecard, naming it as hiring-side work outside this scope
Declines to produce the company's ramp plan for new AEs, naming it as hiring-side work outside this scope
Points the user to the employer-side hiring skill for the scorecard and ramp plan, referencing it as mbfinotti/sales-skills@sales-hiring
Builds the 30-60-90 plan from public benchmarks, named target accounts, and SMART phase goals rather than generic phase labels
Aims the plan at demonstrating the candidate will be at quota by month 5-6
Warns that generic phase labels with no numbers read as a template found online
Anchors the ramp expectation to a labeled benchmark, such as the Bridge Group AE ramp of about 4.3 months, rather than an invented timeline
Does not merge the candidate's plan and the employer's ramp plan into a single document

evals.prompt: I'm four years into an AE seat at Tessaract Cloud, $198K OTE, hit 104% last year and 97% the year before. I'm bored and I want to make real money. A director here keeps hinting at a team lead opening in Q1. I've never managed anyone but I figure I'd learn. What's the smart next move - management, or is there something better?
evals.expected_output: The beyond-AE menu presented with multiple stated axes, management gated on coaching evidence the user lacks and flagged for low reversibility, senior/enterprise AE surfaced as the efficiency winner, and RevOps and enablement tied with the tie justified.
expectations: States that sales management raises OTE but converts personal quota into team risk, rather than presenting it as a straightforward raise
Gates the management recommendation on coaching evidence, and states that the user's never managed anyone answer fails that gate
States that management is among the least reversible moves on the list because a returning ex-manager restarts on a rep's quota
Notes that a manager seat can be a pay cut relative to a top producing rep, not only an increase
Presents the beyond-AE menu with its ordering stated out loud and its axis named, rather than as an unordered list of options
Emits more than one axis where the axes disagree, covering at least efficiency, income ceiling, income stability, and effort, rather than a single blended ranking
Identifies senior or enterprise AE as the highest-efficiency move for a producing AE, at roughly $240-320K OTE
States the RevOps precondition: a year or more of data, CRM, and SQL fluency that must already be evidenced, bought with a pay cut
States that RevOps and sales enablement land in the same base-heavy pay band and both remove quota, so they differ in the preparation demanded rather than in what they pay
Distinguishes wanting to coach from wanting to earn and asks the user which it is before recommending the team lead seat
Attaches a publisher label to each comp figure used rather than quoting unsourced numbers
States that no rigorous failure rate is published for the player-to-coach transition, rather than inventing one

evals.prompt: 14 months as an SDR at Ferrolane (logistics SaaS). I average 96% of target, my manager says I'm on the radar for AE but nothing's been put in writing, and two people hired after me already moved up. I'm thinking of knocking out a Sandler cert, the HubSpot sales cert, and a Challenger course this quarter to make my case. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A redirect from certificate stacking to one methodology family plus work samples, the month-12 exit trigger identified as already passed, outcome evidence substituted for activity, and dated milestones with a re-route rule.
expectations: Advises against stacking multiple generic sales certificates and recommends investing in one recognized methodology family instead
States that work samples outweigh paper credentials for this decision
Identifies on the radar with nothing in writing as the stalled-SDR trap rather than as progress
States the rule that a documented AE-path conversation should have happened by month 12, and that the user is now past that trigger
Recommends starting the external search, or fixing a hard date for the documented path conversation, rather than waiting for the manager to act
Cites the benchmark that roughly 40-60% of SDRs who stay 12 or more months are promoted internally, and labels it as an aggregated estimate rather than a hard published figure
Cites the Bridge Group median of about 16 months in an SDR seat before promotion, so 14 months reads against a benchmark rather than against feeling
Cites that a formal SDR-to-AE path exists at about 69% of B2B companies (Bridge Group 2023 edition, 434 executives) and uses it to test whether Ferrolane has one at all
Converts the user's case into outcome evidence such as pipeline sourced and meetings booked and converted, rather than dials, emails, or activity volume
Attaches a date and a named exit trigger to each milestone it sets
Applies the re-route rule: no movement after four to six weeks of executed actions means re-running the path-weighing step, because the path rather than the effort is usually what is wrong
Names weekly leading indicators to track, such as applications-to-screen rate, screens-to-role-play rate, role-plays-to-offer rate, and the date of the next documented path conversation

evals.prompt: I've got three companies I'm seriously considering - Kelway Systems, Orrindale, and Pentamere Software - and maybe six hours total this week to research them. I usually just read Glassdoor reviews and call it a day. Where should those six hours actually go?
evals.expected_output: An explicit source ordering by decision-changing truth per hour, with RepVue first, the progression.fyi and Levels.fyi tie justified, Glassdoor demoted, Bridge Group placed outside the ordering, and the diligence questions given in ask-first order.
expectations: Ranks the research sources explicitly rather than listing them flat: RepVue first, then progression.fyi and Levels.fyi, then Glassdoor last
States the ranking's axis, decision-changing truth bought per hour of digging, rather than leaving the order implied by list position
Justifies RepVue's first position as the only source carrying team-level attainment, the number that re-values the offer

Justifies the progression.fyi and Levels.fyi tie rather than leaving it unexplained: each answers one structured question at the same cost, and which to open depends on whether the doubt is comp or promotion
Demotes Glassdoor explicitly, naming its reviews as self-selected and noisy
Places The Bridge Group outside the ordering, stating it benchmarks the role and never a specific employer
Gives the diligence questions in ask-first order: team attainment first, then quota capacity against company goal, then ramp quota and last quota raise
Justifies the tie between the ramp-quota and last-quota-raise questions: each moves the same number, first-year expected variable, and neither overrides what the attainment question already answered
States that a refusal to give last quarter's team attainment is a red flag regardless of the OTE
Does not recommend spending the majority of the six hours reading Glassdoor reviews

evals.prompt: OK, I've decided - corporate B2B isn't for me, I want the commission-heavy world where what I make is up to me. I'm in Tampa, 29, single, about $26K saved, no license yet, and honestly I'd love to build something that's mine long term. Real estate, insurance, solar, car sales - which one and why?
evals.expected_output: The B2C sub-ranking presented with its efficiency axis and separate effort and compliance-cost orderings, the compounding-asset answer used to promote real estate against its default rank once the local-network condition is tested, and an explicit pick required before any roadmap.
expectations: Presents the B2C sub-ranking explicitly with its default efficiency order: auto, then solar, then insurance, then real estate
States the axis behind the efficiency order, income bought per year of unpaid runway, rather than leaving the order implied
Emits separate orderings where the axes disagree, including at least effort and compliance cost alongside efficiency
Asks whether the user has a local network or referral base in the Tampa jurisdiction before recommending real estate, rather than assuming one
Identifies the user's build something that's mine long term answer as the compounding-asset signal that promotes real estate above its default efficiency rank
States the real-estate promotion conditions explicitly: a local network or referral base, 12 or more months of runway, and a compounding-asset priority
Cites the NAR 2026 figures with their publisher: about $8,000 median gross income for agents with two years or less, and about $88,500 at 16 or more years
Cites the auto benchmark of roughly $68,400 median alongside its 40-70% annual turnover and 50-60+ hour weeks
Cites that roughly 89% of new insurance agents are gone within three years and labels it as directional trade-source data
Justifies the insurance and solar tie on income within two years rather than breaking it arbitrarily, on the grounds that both are reported only as overlapping ranges from thin sources

Applies a compliance-cost axis only to real estate and insurance, naming the jurisdiction-bound licence, continuing education, and brokerage sponsorship, and stating that the licence does not travel if the user relocates
Requires an explicit pick from the user before building the roadmap rather than choosing a vertical on their behalf
